RunTheTasksOfABenchmark
A maintainer lists the benchmark's tasks, commits its data and runs five of them. The plain task copies the data
    with no remote and hands its steps the merged config, once driving the checkout in place and once on a pinned clone
    behind a fence. The override task lays its config over the base. The scored task prints its score. The library task
    calls the helpers a task module imports. They keep each result and read its ledger and score.

ARoundIsInterruptedAndResumed
A step stops the interrupt round after its first step. No result is written, so there is nothing to keep. The
    maintainer resumes it: the first step keeps its outcome, the other two run, and the ledger then holds both
    segments. A second resume has no open round left and a numbered one that was never made is refused.

ARoundStoppedFromOutside\nA maintainer starts the interrupt task by hand and its round is stopped before the last two steps, as Ctrl-C\n    would stop it. They resume it, the first step keeps its outcome and the other two run, and they keep the result.

AStepFails
A maintainer runs a task that does not fail and then the three tasks that fail on purpose. A step that raises is printed with its error and the
    steps after it are skipped. A step that reads a boolean input as a number fails on its type. A command that is not
    installed fails the step that runs it. Each round still writes a result, whose ledger names the failed and skipped
    steps.

WrongTurns
A maintainer runs paddock out of order. A run before the data has a commit is refused. After the commit, a
    benchmark the root does not hold and a task the benchmark does not declare are refused, and so is a resume with no
    round, with a round number that was never made, and with a round that already has its result.

ABenchmarkThatDoesNotLoad
A maintainer lists the benchmarks, adds one whose tasks.py raises, and lists again: the good benchmark's tasks
    are still printed and the exit is 1. A benchmark name is still refused with both benchmarks named. They then point
    paddock_dir at a folder with no gold/: the list says there are no benchmarks and a run names none.
TheHomeConfigIsWrong\nA maintainer leaves the home config as text that is not TOML. List, run and resume all stop with exit 2 and the\n    parser's message, before they read the root.

TheSandboxRefusesWhatWouldLeak
A maintainer sets up a sandboxed book run. The command after `--` is needed, the config must be readable and
    may only name claude or opencode, and each login it names must exist. Each app must exist and carry its own
    directory name. With several apps the command must say which one it starts in, and that name must be one of them.
    Every refusal comes before docker is asked for anything.
- **uncommitted**: the benchmark's data folder holds files and is not a git repository. Reached by: a fresh service, nothing done.
- **ready**: the data folder is a git repository with a commit and no round has run. Reached by: CommitTheData.
- **ran**: the plain task ran once and left a result. Reached by: CommitTheData; paddock run acme plain --no-pin-project --quiet.
- **interrupted**: the interrupt task stopped after its first step and left a round to resume. Reached by: CommitTheData; StopARound.
- **a-broken-benchmark**: a second benchmark whose tasks.py raises sits beside acme. Reached by: CommitTheData; AddABrokenBenchmark.
- **empty-root**: paddock_dir names a folder with no gold/. Reached by: EmptyTheRoot.
- **home-config-broken**: the home config is not TOML. Reached by: BreakTheHomeConfig.

`paddock run` writes its step lines to stdout and exits 1 when a step failed, and writes its errors to stderr and
exits 1 when it never started. A command declares one shape per exit code, so one class cannot say both. RunTask
declares exit 1 as stderr and keeps to tasks whose steps all pass, and RunTaskThatFails declares exit 1 as the stdout
lines and keeps to tasks whose steps fail. The argv is the same, with the benchmark fixed to acme.
A refusal that comes before the first step leaves nothing on stdout, so RunTaskThatFails words it as the empty message.
Its refusals are only the ones its columns can reach.

sources: paddock/paddock/project.py::pin, paddock/paddock/project.py::release
Without --no-pin-project a round drives a remoteless clone of the checkout paddock is imported from, checked out detached
at its HEAD, with its git directory stashed beside it and `.git` replaced by a gitfile that names a path that does not
exist (paddock/paddock/project.py::pin, fence). The clone costs a few seconds, so the book plays it once in a column
and once in a journey, and every other play passes --no-pin-project. The plain task's second step writes what it sees
of the pin: that it is pinned, that it is fenced and that it has no remote. Release deletes the clone when the round
ends.
The pinned round shows `pinned=True` in its note and `"pinned": true` in the ledger. The unpinned one shows both as
False, and has no fence to look at.

paddock logs `run <name>` at INFO as its first act once a round is reserved, so every error after that point has a
stderr that starts with lines naming the stablemate sha. Those refusals cannot be quoted word for word and are not
played: a score() that edits the staged tree (paddock/paddock/runner.py::_score, the manifest guard), a score() that
returns something other than a Score, and a base home-config.toml that is not TOML or fails the config schema
(paddock/paddock/homeconfig.py::materialize). Their code is named by RunTask's source.
The refusals that come before that log line are played, and they are the ones a person meets most: no such benchmark,
no such task, a data folder with no commit, and a home config that does not parse.

A round's result lives under results/<benchmark>/<task>/<data commit>-<stablemate sha>/<n>/. The stablemate sha is
the HEAD of the checkout paddock is imported from, so the path differs on every machine and after every commit, and
a watch cannot name it. The book reads what a round did through two other doors.
The first is the tasks themselves. Each step writes a note under <sandbox>/seen/ with the facts a reader of the
README would want shown: the stage holds the data files and no remote, the config is the base with the task's
override laid over it, a relative artifacts_dir names a folder inside the stage, the pin is a clone behind a fence
with no remote, the inputs read through the helpers. Each note is a file the watch lists with the lines it holds.
The second is a person copying a result out of results/ by hand, which the README says to do to keep one. The
KeepTheResults event copies the latest ledger.json and score.json of each task into kept/, and the watch lists which
statuses, segments and caveats each holds. A round that ends in a step failure, a resume or an interruption still shows
as it did.
The lines paddock prints for a step carry its seconds with one decimal. A step that only reads files takes under
fifty milliseconds, so its line is `0.0s`. The only step that starts a process is the one that runs `false`, and it
is the slowest of them.

A step that raises the runner's RoundInterrupted ends `paddock run` with exit 130 and no result. The workspace keeps
round.json and steps.json, and `paddock resume` finds the highest round that has no result and runs only the steps
without an ok outcome (paddock/paddock/runner.py::_unfinished_workspace, resume). The ledger it writes then holds
both segments, `interrupted` and `finished`.
The 130 answer declares no stdout. Its message goes to stderr, where it names the round by the data commit and the
stablemate sha, and the sha differs per checkout, so the book does not quote it. The rule for it says only that
the round is left open.
A scene cannot be arranged by a step the app refuses, and 130 is a refusal. The scene `interrupted` is reached by the
StopARound event, which starts the interrupt task by hand and lets the model take the same change a refused run
makes. A column and a journey step still call RunTask on the interrupt task, which is where the 130 is judged.
The interrupt task passes its second step only once it finds its own note from the first attempt. A run of the task
after that note exists therefore finishes in one go, which is why the model reads the note.

paddock.tasks holds the helpers a benchmark's tasks module imports. The book plays the ones a step can run with no
agent: inputs (names, number, flag), judge.render, forensics.entered_nodes and cycles, operator_gates.record_hand_answer
and its reads, and tree.stage_members and repos_at. The library task calls them and writes what they returned.
greenfield, replay and the stablemate helpers drive workhorse and an agent CLI for minutes, run uv, farrier and git
over the stage and spend a budget, and judge.call_agent calls a model. A play must not start them, so RunTask names
their files in its source and says nothing of what they print. A benchmark that uses them states its own score.

The book plays paddock against a sandbox that is a benchmark root. The home config names it with paddock_dir, and
under it gold/acme holds the base home-config.toml, a tasks.py of eight small tasks and a data folder. Each task
exists to show one behaviour of a round: the copy of the data, the merged config, the inputs, a failing step, a
command that fails, a score, an interruption and the helpers a task module imports. The benchmark is named by its folder under gold/, and its data folder is
named data because paddock reads it by that name (paddock/paddock/paths.py, DATA).
The data folder must be a git repository with a commit before a round can copy it. The seed cannot carry a .git
folder, so a person commits it with the CommitTheData event, and the scene `uncommitted` is the one before.
The surface puts the bin folder of the interpreter that runs ostler first on PATH, so that `paddock` is the copy
installed beside it and not whichever one the caller's PATH finds first (a pipx copy on a machine can fail to import).
The environment holds that PATH, HOME, STABLEMATE_CONFIG and the git identity the commit needs, and nothing else of the
machine.

sources: paddock/paddock/cli.py::cmd_sandbox_build, paddock/paddock/sandbox.py::build, paddock/paddock/sandbox.py::Sandbox.refusals
`paddock sandbox run` checks, in order, that a command follows `--`, that the config reads and names only agent CLIs
the sandbox has a login for, that no mount is missing or duplicated or holds the stablemate checkout, and that
--workdir names one of the apps (paddock/paddock/cli.py::cmd_sandbox_run, paddock/paddock/sandbox.py). A call that
passes all of them hands the container to docker and returns docker's exit code. The book plays every refusal and
never the pass, so the success answer and the input classes are declared unseen: docker, its image and its daemon are
the machine's, not the app's.
`paddock sandbox build` is not a command of the book. It runs `uv build --all-packages` over the checkout and then
docker build, takes the agent CLI releases from the machine, and cannot be played without starting both. Its code is
named in this decision's sources.
The check for a mount that holds the checkout is not played either, since it needs a path that holds the checkout of
whoever runs the book.
RunTask: why does a tasks.py that raises on import end a run in a traceback when list reports the same error as "cannot load" and carries on?
